Extensions

overlay + keyboard

Both extensions on simulated glass. The phone below is inside some other app — a job form, a recruiter thread — and Reel rides over it: the overlay on Android, the keyboard on iOS. The vault comes preloaded as Alex Rivera, a demo applicant; anything you add stays in this browser only. A webpage can't reach into real apps, so judge the speed and the feel here, not the reach.

The overlay · Android Being built · simulated here

Apply to Northbeam using only the overlay

The phone is inside Northbeam's careers app. The round button on its edge is Reel — it floats over whatever app you're in. Fill the whole application without ever leaving the form.

No overlays on iOS — the overlay is Android's. On iPad the vault rides the keyboard, the share sheet, and the Files app instead.

The moves

Tap the round buttonOpens and stays. Copied something just before? The overlay catches it — or offers to, depending on the catch switch below. Spin the ring: it steps one item at a time and settles — a fast flick carries a few extra clicks; the item at the index mark is up. Tap it — copied, receipt, and the box you were in grows a Paste chip: tap that and the job is done. Tap the glass centre to put the overlay away.
One ring, everything on itYour two pinned items hold the edge slots — same place forever, tap to use — and everything else follows, newest first, all types together. Colour says the type: amber is text, rust is a link, violet is an image.
Hold · slide out · releaseOne finger, never lifting. Hold the button and slide out onto the ring, then arc your finger to spin it. Release on an item to take it and put the overlay away.
Hold · dragDrag the button anywhere and let go — it clings to the nearest frame edge, at the height you left it, and stays there.
Double-tap the buttonYour most recent item, instantly. No ring, no aiming.
Hold — it comes to youHold, and the ring comes to you. Hold an off-center item and the ring walks it to the index mark, then stops. Hold either end of the arc — or drag past it and stay — and the ring keeps cruising from that end, gathering speed, until you let go.

The panel below changes how the overlay feels. Flip one switch, run the errand again.

The first pretends you copied something elsewhere; the second replays the one-time permission moment. Add a photo and it joins the overlay; add a document and it shows up when you attach inside the form — the file never leaves this browser, only its name is remembered.

Select any text on this page and a Save to Reel chip appears — write a line of your own cover letter, save it, then reuse it on the keyboard page.

The keyboard · iOS Concept exhibit

Second application of the day — this time on the iPhone

This is the iOS surface: your stuff rides the keyboard. Tap into any box on the phone and the vault comes up first — you drop in, take what you came for, and leave. Swipe left and the keys page is a faithful twin of the iPhone keyboard — same shapes, same moves, same feel — with one strip of your stuff where the suggestions would be. On Android the overlay carries this job instead.

This keyboard is iPhone and iPad. The frame you picked is Android hardware — there, the overlay is how the vault travels.

Five things to try

Tap a box, tap a tileThe vault opens first — pins up front, newest after, everything in one strip. A tile lands right at your cursor, done. A box that can't take a thing just dims it: tap into Email and watch the images grey out; the message box lights everything back up.
Swipe left — the keysA faithful twin of the iPhone keyboard. Keys balloon when you press them, tap shift twice for CAPS, hold e for accents, 123 and #+= for numbers and symbols, two quick spaces end a sentence. Your vault rides the strip above the keys — tap a chip and it lands at the cursor. The gear tunes sounds and the return key.
X-ray itFlip X-ray below and every part says who owns it: green is ours, blue is Apple's design rebuilt by us, and rust marks what only Apple's own keyboard can have — password autofill, codes from Messages, dictation. Those stay ghosts on ours, by iOS's rules, which is why leaving is one tap.
Tap the password boxiOS hands passwords to Apple's own keyboard, automatically. Watch the swap — nothing custom ever sees a password.
LeaveOne tap on back to your keyboard — or the globe under the keys — and you're typing on your own again. iOS brings up whichever keyboard you used last, so a fast exit is part of the design.

Also here: search runs on our own keys (a keyboard can't summon a keyboard), and the Interview thanks tile asks you to fill a blank before it inserts. Replay the first run below shows the one-time Full Access moment — try both answers. On the iPad frame the keys widen into the iPad arrangement, with the tuck-away key at the bottom corner.
